course.title: Writing and Storytelling
course.tagline: Write stories people remember: characters, plot and endings that land.

days.title: What makes a good story?
days.goal: Say what makes a story worth reading.
steps: Watch today's video and write down the main idea about what makes a good story: a person, a problem and a change in your notebook.
Write for 15 minutes using what makes a good story: a person, a problem and a change — aim for one full page, not perfection.
Read what you wrote aloud and circle the three weakest sentences.
Rewrite those three sentences using what makes a good story: a person, a problem and a change more deliberately.
Share today's writing with one person and ask what they remember most.
days.task: Write down your three favourite stories and what you like about each.
days.challenge: Tell a friend in one minute why your favourite story works.

quiz.q: What does every good story need?
options: A person, a problem and a change.
Ten characters.
A long description.
A happy ending.
quiz.explain: Every good story has a person, a problem they face, and a change by the end.

quiz.q: Which of these is the goal of today's lesson?
options: Write a full scene with action and talk.
Say what makes a story worth reading.
Build a side character who helps or blocks your hero.
Start a second story with a new idea.
quiz.explain: Today's lesson is about What makes a good story? — its goal is: Say what makes a story worth reading.

quiz.q: Which of these did today's lesson focus on?
options: planning a story: start, middle, end
building tension: questions, delays and danger
fixing plot holes
what makes a good story: a person, a problem and a change
quiz.explain: Today's focus was what makes a good story: a person, a problem and a change.

options: Real life: things you felt, saw or wished for.

Only from the news.
quiz.explain: Real life gives the best ideas: things you felt, saw or wished for.

The same character in every story.
The same length for every story.

days.goal: Read a story and steal one trick from it.

Write for 15 minutes using reading like a writer — aim for one full page, not perfection.

days.challenge: Use one of those tricks in your own story.

quiz.q: What does 'read like a writer' mean?
options: Notice how the writer built the story, not just what happened.
Read very fast.
Read only the ending.
Read with a pen in your mouth.
quiz.explain: Reading like a writer means noticing how the story was built, so you can use the same tricks.

quiz.q: Which of these is the goal of today's lesson?

Give your character a problem worth solving.

sharing your work with readers
finding story ideas from real life
showing feelings through action
quiz.explain: Today's focus was reading like a writer.

days.title: Get feedback
days.goal: Ask for feedback and use it.
steps: Watch today's video and write down the main idea about getting feedback on your writing in your notebook.
Write for 15 minutes using getting feedback on your writing — aim for one full page, not perfection.
Read what you wrote aloud and circle the three weakest sentences.

Share today's writing with one person and ask what they remember most.

days.challenge: Fix the one thing both readers named.

quiz.q: What is the best way to take feedback?
options: Listen, thank them, and fix what makes the story better.
Argue with every comment.
Ignore all feedback.
Rewrite the whole story each time.
quiz.explain: Listen, thank them, and fix what makes the story better. You do not have to fix everything.

quiz.q: Which of these is the goal of today's lesson?

Plan your story in three parts.
Keep readers guessing about what happens next.
Ask for feedback and use it.

getting feedback on your writing
building a main character: want, flaw and strength
writing real dialogue

days.title: Write every day
days.goal: Build a daily writing habit.
steps: Watch today's video and write down the main idea about building a daily writing habit in your notebook.
Write for 15 minutes using building a daily writing habit — aim for one full page, not perfection.
Read what you wrote aloud and circle the three weakest sentences.

Share today's writing with one person and ask what they remember most.

quiz.q: What matters most in a writing habit?
options: Showing up every day, even for a short time.
Writing for five hours once a week.
Waiting for inspiration.
Writing only when you feel like it.
quiz.explain: Showing up every day matters most. Short daily writing beats long rare writing.

quiz.q: Which of these is the goal of today's lesson?
options: Build a daily writing habit.
Plan your next 30 days of writing.
Write an opening that pulls people in.
Write the middle of your story.

giving your character a problem
building a daily writing habit
describing with the five senses

The commas.
The font.
The title.
quiz.explain: Fix the story first: does it make sense? Then fix sentences. Spelling comes last.

planning a story: start, middle, end
building tension: questions, delays and danger
editing in three passes

Sharing is only for famous writers.
Sharing makes your writing worse.
You should never share.

capstone.title: The Storyteller
capstone.brief: Write a complete short story of 1,500 words or more, with a main character, a real problem, a middle where things get harder, and an ending that shows change. Share it with three readers.
checks: Your story is 1,500 words or more
Your main character has a want and a flaw
Your story has a clear problem
Your middle makes things harder
Your ending shows change
You used showing, not telling, in at least three places
Three people read your story and gave feedback
deliverables: A complete short story of 1,500 words or more
A one-page plan of the story: character, problem, start, middle, end
A second short story of 300 words or more
A list of feedback from three readers
A short note on what you will write next
